baseline.text: Only the first ratio is a measurement. Its risk leg is the premium minus what the contract would still be worth at the stock stop, which depends on strike, spot, time and IV independently — so it genuinely differs between contracts. The greyed one divides two numbers that are both a fixed fraction of premium, so premium cancels out of it entirely and nothing about this contract survives into the result. It is the same on every contract you could pick, which is why it is greyed. Deliberately not written as a division of the two percentages shown above: both are rounded for display while the stop fraction is an arbitrary number, so working it out from them disagrees with the printed ratio on roughly two rows in five.

disclosures: How these exit settings are resolved
baseline.text: Premium stop is a loss amount per share. Its premium basis is the live mid when one is available, otherwise the scan mid, otherwise the plan's entry limit — the same basis that bounds the field. An untouched field shows the global percentage applied to the live mid; a typed or restored amount is kept until you clear it. Monte Carlo and Arithmetic premiums are separate calculation inputs and are never used here. The opened position resolves the stop against its actual fill: a typed dollar amount stays fixed, while an inherited global percentage is applied to the fill.

It is priced with the time to expiry left on that day, so time decay is included. {{stopCostShown ? ( <> {' '}For the immediate figure — what this stop costs if it is hit right now — see “Max loss if the stop is hit” in Structure & Stops. The two differ by time decay AND can differ by volatility input: both are Black-Scholes prices at the stop, but that one uses today's full time to expiry (no time decay), its loss is not capped, and it takes the supplied implied volatility or one solved from the mid, while these use the time left at the repricing day and the volatility the simulation solved from the mid (or its fallback). Both are correct; naming only the decay sent a hand-checker looking for a difference decay alone cannot account for. </> ) : null}}

baseline.text: Only the first ratio is a measurement. Its risk leg is the premium minus what the contract would still be worth at the stock stop, which depends on strike, spot, time and IV independently — so it genuinely differs between contracts. The greyed one divides two numbers that are both a fixed fraction of premium, so premium cancels out of it entirely and nothing about this contract survives into the result. It is the same on every contract you could pick, which is why it is greyed. Deliberately not written as a division of the two percentages shown above: both are rounded for display while the stop fraction is an arbitrary number, so working it out from them disagrees with the printed ratio on roughly two rows in five.

disclosures: How these exit settings are resolved
baseline.text: Premium stop is a loss amount per share. Its premium basis is the live mid when one is available, otherwise the scan mid, otherwise the plan's entry limit — the same basis that bounds the field. An untouched field shows the global percentage applied to the live mid; a typed or restored amount is kept until you clear it. Monte Carlo and Arithmetic premiums are separate calculation inputs and are never used here. The opened position resolves the stop against its actual fill: a typed dollar amount stays fixed, while an inherited global percentage is applied to the fill.
